title: In which cases does @Transactional NOT roll back (checked exceptions, self-invocation, private methods, swallowed exceptions), and what are the common pitfalls?
keyPoints: Checked exceptions (IOException, PaymentGatewayException) cause a COMMIT, not a rollback, by default
Only RuntimeException and Error trigger automatic rollback -- fix with rollbackFor = Exception.class
Self-invocation (this.method()) bypasses the proxy, so the @Transactional annotation is ignored
Private methods cannot be proxied by CGLIB -- the annotation is silently ignored
Catching and swallowing an exception makes the proxy see a normal return, so it commits
Fix swallowed exceptions by re-throwing or calling setRollbackOnly() on the current transaction status
These four pitfalls cause silent data corruption because no error is reported to the caller

s1_definition.oneliner: @Transactional silently fails to roll back in four cases: checked exceptions commit by default, self-invocation bypasses the proxy, private methods are ignored, and swallowed exceptions cause a commit.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Checked exceptions** -- by default, `@Transactional` rolls back only on `RuntimeException` and `Error`. A checked exception like `IOException` or `PaymentGatewayException` causes the proxy to COMMIT the transaction, potentially leaving half-finished data.
- **Self-invocation** -- calling a `@Transactional` method from within the same class with `this.method()` goes directly to the real object and bypasses the Spring proxy. No transaction is started.
- **Private methods** -- Spring uses CGLIB to create a subclass proxy. A subclass cannot override a `private` method, so the `@Transactional` annotation is silently ignored.
- **Swallowed exceptions** -- if you catch an exception inside the method without re-throwing, the proxy sees a normal method return and COMMITS the partial work.
- **Fix** -- use `rollbackFor = Exception.class`, extract methods to separate beans, make methods public, and always re-throw or call `setRollbackOnly()`.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the vault door (proxy) only auto-closes on fire alarms (RuntimeException), not on smoke alarms (checked exceptions). If a teller asks himself to lock the vault (self-invocation), he just talks to himself and the vault mechanism never activates. The vault door only works on public entrances, not private back doors. And if a teller catches the fire alarm and silences it (swallowed exception), the vault door thinks everything is fine and stays open.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Normal @Transactional flow (proxy intercepts)            │
│                                                           │
│  Caller ──► Proxy ──► Real Object                        │
│              │         │                                  │
│         BEGIN TX       execute method()                   │
│              │         │                                  │
│              │    normal return ──► COMMIT                │
│              │    RuntimeException ──► ROLLBACK           │
│              │    checked exception ──► COMMIT (!)        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Self-invocation (proxy BYPASSED)                         │
│                                                           │
│  Caller ──► Proxy ──► Real Object                        │
│                         │                                 │
│                    this.otherMethod()                     │
│                         │                                 │
│                    Real Object.otherMethod()              │
│                    (no proxy, no TX)                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Fix: separate bean (proxy intercepts)                    │
│                                                           │
│  Caller ──► Proxy-A ──► ServiceA                         │
│                           │                               │
│                    otherService.method()                  │
│                           │                               │
│               Proxy-B ──► ServiceB.method()               │
│                │                                          │
│           BEGIN TX    execute method()    COMMIT/ROLLBACK │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
There are four cases where @Transactional silently fails to roll back, and each one causes data corruption without any visible error. Checked exceptions commit by default because only RuntimeException and Error trigger rollback. Self-invocation bypasses the proxy because calling this.method() goes directly to the real object. Private methods are ignored because CGLIB cannot override them. Swallowed exceptions cause a commit because the proxy sees a normal method return.

In Rajesh's EMI payment service at the National Bank of India, the checked-exception pitfall was the most dangerous. A PaymentGatewayException (checked) caused the transaction to commit even though the payment gateway was down. The EMI was marked as processed in the database, but the payment never actually went through. The customer's balance was deducted with no payment made. Adding `rollbackFor = Exception.class` to every @Transactional annotation in the codebase became a standard practice.

Pankaj, the architect, enforces four defensive rules: always use rollbackFor = Exception.class, never call @Transactional methods from within the same class, never put @Transactional on private methods, and never catch exceptions inside a transactional method without re-throwing or calling setRollbackOnly(). ArchUnit tests enforce the public-method rule automatically.

Remember one sentence: @Transactional rolls back only on RuntimeException by default, so always add rollbackFor = Exception.class and never bypass the proxy.
